newsitem.title: USA: US Southeast power plummets ahead of mild weekend.
newsitem.headline: US Southeast power plummets ahead of mild weekend.

text.p: Spot electricity prices in the southeastern U.S. cratered Friday in congruence with natural gas prices as milder weather was forecast for the weekend and early next week and several generating plants returned to service, sources said.

Firm, peak power prices in the northern part of the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) territory for Monday were sharply lower in the $16.00-17.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) range, as compared with Thursday's $39.00-41.00 trading range.
Firm, off-peak electricity in northern TVA was notionally assessed at $11.00-13.00, but no deals could be confirmed done.

At the Georgia/Florida border, prices for firm, peak electricity in 16 hour blocks for Monday delivery plummeted into the $24.00-25.00 range, as compared with the $42.00-43.00 trading range on Thursday.
Firm, off-peak power for Monday at the Ga./Fla. border was notionally assessed at $12.00-13.00, but sources said trading extremely light.

In Florida, peak power prices on a 16-hour schedule for Monday were about $20 lower in the $25.00 per MWh area. Despite cold weather now in northern Florida, the thermometer is expected to climb into the 50s and 60s Saturday, the National Weather Service reported.
Temperatures throughout the Southeast are expected moderate this weekend, but another cold front is expected to land in the area by midweek.
Sources attributed the sharp decline in prices to an expected drop in demand next week because of the Christmas holiday.
Like power prices, natural gas spot values in south Texas fell by about 30 cents today to the low-$4.20s per million British thermal units.
Separately, Carolina Power and Light's 880 megawatt (MW) Harris 1 nuclear power unit in New Hill, N.C., shut late Thursday, was expected to return to service by this afternoon.
Also, Virginia Power's Surry 2 (781 MW) and North Anna 2 (909 MW) nuclear units are expected to return to the grid on Monday at the latest.
The 1,129 MW Catawba 2 nuclear unit in Clover, S.C., remains shut and is expected to restart either this weekend or early next week.
